headline: Ballistic Ventures Raises $490M to Fight AI With More AI
subheadline: Cybersecurity fund launches at peak hype, betting that this time the category won't crater in 36 months.
source_headline: Ted Schlein's Ballistic Ventures seeks $490M for new funds amid AI-driven cybersecurity boom
body_html:
Ballistic Ventures, the cybersecurity-focused fund led by Ted Schlein, is raising $490 million across two vehicles: a $360 million flagship fund and a $130 million separate investment vehicle. The timing is exquisite. We are, as near as anyone can tell, at the exact peak of AI-driven investor desperation, where every sector from agricultural drones to tax software is being retrofitted with machine learning and suddenly worth three times its previous valuation. Cybersecurity, long a reliable category for VC returns, has apparently decided to join the AI fever dream.

Ballistic Ventures has been around long enough to know what it's doing—this isn't some first-time fund manager chasing momentum. The firm has built a track record in cybersecurity investing, a category that actually generates revenue and solves real problems, which is refreshing in venture capital circles. But here's the thing: cybersecurity already works. Companies already pay for it. The category doesn't need AI to justify itself, which means adding AI to the pitch is less about fundamental innovation and more about making the fund's $490 million check seem proportionate to the moment's frothy sentiment.

This is VC's cyclical ritual: identify a category that works, wait for the market to get bored with it, then rebrand it with whatever technology the CNBC ticker is screaming about. Schlein and his team have been through booms and busts before. They know that if you can attach "AI-driven" to your fund strategy, LPs will increase their checks by roughly 40 percent. The question is not whether Ballistic is competent—it almost certainly is—but whether the market's current AI euphoria will still be priced in by the time most of this capital is deployed.

The press release, one can safely assume, will emphasize language like "AI-augmented threat detection" and "machine learning-powered incident response," which are real capabilities with real value that existed in slightly different forms two years ago. The genius of the rebrand is that it's not entirely dishonest; it's just emphasizing the shiniest part of an already functional strategy. Throw enough venture capital at something, and you can make it sound revolutionary, even if the underlying business logic hasn't changed since 2019.

What could go wrong? Everything, potentially. If AI winters arrive faster than expected, or if enterprise security budgets contract due to economic headwinds, a $490 million fund optimized for the current cycle could find itself chasing deals in a market that has already moved on—or worse, consolidated. Cybersecurity is not a "hit-driven" category like consumer apps; most exits are in the $500M to $2B range. Deploying nearly half a billion dollars into that outcome distribution is mathematically challenging, even for excellent investors.

The broader pattern here is worth noting: we are now seeing late-stage, respectable funds raise massive amounts of capital based on trends that may have already peaked. This is what the tail end of a venture cycle looks like—not reckless first-timers, but disciplined operators deciding that the momentum is too strong to resist. When everyone good is raising larger funds than they would have two years ago, it's usually a sign that capital is about to become slightly less scarce, and multiples are about to compress.

Ballistic will probably make money. Some of their bets will work. But ask again in 2028 whether a $490 million fund designed for the AI-cybersecurity convergence thesis was actually necessary, or just the logical outcome of a market that couldn't resist one more mega-round before sanity returned.
glossary_definition: Any existing product or service that engineers have added a neural network to and marketing has tripled the price of.
